title: CBA warns of record year-long 15pc price slump
full_text:
The Commonwealth Bank says it expects the country's housing market to experience its largest downturn ever, with prices plunging in every capital city including Sydney, where they will fall as much as 16 per cent.
The alarming forecast was published hours before the Reserve Bank of Australia lifted the official cash rate for the fifth time this year to an 18-year high of 4.85 per cent, and warned it could increase further next year.
In a note, economists at the country's biggest home lender said the interest rate outlook had "moved against the housing market", prompting it to downgrade its view only two months after its last forecast because of what it said was "a faster and broader correction than expected".
The correction will be most severe in once-booming markets such as Perth and Brisbane, where the CBA is forecasting peak-to-trough declines of 18 per cent. Prices are tipped to drop 13 per cent in Melbourne and Adelaide.
And the bank does not expect prices to bottom until late next year, when the average value of a home across the capital cities will have fallen 15 per cent.
The combination of higher interest rates and the Albanese government's changes to property tax concessions - including capital gains and negative gearing - have already put home values on track for their fastest decline in four decades. Widely cited figures published by Cotality this week showed that Sydney property prices had fallen 10.1 per cent between their February peak and the end of October, while Perth values were down 8.9 per cent.
Economists at CBA said that if their forecasts were correct, the downturn would be "the largest decline in national dwelling prices in the history of the monthly series, which extends back around 45 years".
"Sydney has experienced the deepest correction to date, with values 10.1 per cent below their February peak, while Melbourne is 8.2 per cent below its previous peak. But the most striking development ... has been how quickly the downturn has picked up pace in Brisbane and Perth," they wrote.
"We expect the market to stabilise in the second half of 2027, supported by lower dwelling prices and higher rental yields, underlying supply tightness, and the eventual easing in monetary policy.
"However, we do not forecast a material recovery and there remains uncertainty over the ... rate outlook."
Falling prices and rising borrowing costs are stifling demand from buyers. Fewer than half the homes listed for auction over the weekend changed hands as the preliminary clearance rate tumbled to its lowest since April 2020 when the pandemic disrupted public auction markets.
The RBA said that while higher rates were affecting all borrowers, the decline in new lending "has been most pronounced for investors and has been concentrated in loans to purchase established dwellings".
RBA governor Michele Bullock said that the government's housing tax changes had driven investors out of the market more than interest rate rises.
"The fact that investors have declined so much further than [they have] in previous interest rate increasing cycles suggests that there's something else going on here, and that something else going on is the tax changes," she said.
Speaking ahead of the RBA's decision on Tuesday, Treasurer Jim Chalmers said that interest rates were the driving force of the property price falls and stood by Treasury forecasts that the government's changes would only create a 2 per cent slowdown in national house price growth.
"There's certainly been a lot of volatility in the housing market that began before the budget ... and one of the big drivers of that is that people are very worried about interest rates," he told the ABC's Radio National. "The forecasts or the assumptions that are in the budget from the Treasury around house prices are about the next couple of years, not the last couple of months. If you look at some of the private sector forecasts for housing, they expect house price growth to continue from next year."
Despite the long slump in house prices this year, successive interest rate rises have pushed would-be first home buyers to the sidelines.
In Melbourne, warehouse manager Oskar Halperin said he had put his attempts to buy a home on hold until rates had started to fall.
"That just means a whole government change because Labor do not know how to spend their money," Halperin said. "I just want to be able to own property. It's a good investment into my future. I want stability in my life. I want to be able to live somewhere and call it my own home."
In Melbourne, Loan Market mortgage broker Fiona McLean said an average $500,000 property had dropped about $30,000 this year while about $50,000 had been wiped off prospective buyer borrowing capacities.
"It's really hard. It's so heartbreaking to watch because first-home buyers are typically at the lower end of income and affordability so they are most hard hit when they're looking to purchase," McLean said, adding that parents were discouraging their children from buying in a falling market.
Domain's chief residential economist Nicola Powell said that modelling by the listing platform suggested each 25-basis point increase in interest rates reduced borrowing capacity by about 2.5 per cent. "The cumulative impact is becoming increasingly important. Higher mortgage repayments also reduce household disposable income, while weaker borrowing capacity puts a brake on buyer demand," she said.
"Markets where buyers are more constrained by borrowing capacity are likely to be more sensitive to further increases, while stronger income and population growth and tight supply can provide some offset."
Nine Entertainment Co.
